title: The `while` loop repeats as long as the condition is True.
when_to_show: When determining the number of iterations and the termination condition for a `while` loop
body: A `while` loop repeatedly executes the same block of code as long as the condition is `True`.
detail: Whereas a `for` loop iterates through a fixed list in order, the number of iterations in a `while` loop is determined by when the condition becomes `False`. When reading `while` code, you should check the initial variable value, the condition, and how the values affecting the condition change within the loop. This card serves as a supplementary guide to help you understand how loop flow and loop constructs work in actual code.

title: In a `while` loop, the `update` line that changes the condition is important.
when_to_show: When you see a line like `i = i + 1` inside a `while` loop
body: In a `while` loop, an update statement like `i = i + 1` is essential for terminating the loop.
detail: If `i` starts at 0 and the condition is `i < 3`, `i` must be incremented within the loop so that the condition eventually evaluates to `False`. The execution result may vary depending on whether the update statement is inside or outside the loop. This card serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how loop flow and loop constructs work in actual code.

title: "break" stops the loop, and "continue" skips to the next iteration.
when_to_show: When a `break` or `continue` is encountered inside a loop
body: `break` and `continue` are keywords that alter the flow within a loop. `break` immediately terminates the entire loop, while `continue` skips the remaining lines of the current iteration and moves on to the next one.
detail: Since both are frequently used within `if` statements, you must verify under what conditions they operate. This card serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how loop flow and loop constructs are executed in actual code. When solving problems, clearly identify the loop’s starting value, the condition, the current value of the loop variable, the `update` line, and the conditions for `break` and `continue`.

title: `sorted` creates a new, sorted result
when_to_show: When distinguishing between the sorted result and the original list
body: `sorted` is a function that returns a new result with the values sorted. Given `nums = [3, 1, 2]`, `sorted(nums)` returns `[1, 2, 3]`, but the original `nums` itself remains unchanged.
detail: In contrast, `list.sort()` modifies the list itself. This card serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how looping logic and looping tools work in actual code. When solving problems, clearly distinguish the loop’s starting value, the loop condition, the current value of the loop variable, the `update` line, and the `break` and `continue` conditions.

title: "reversed" produces a result that is the reverse of the original sequence.
body: `reversed` is a tool that allows you to read ordered values, such as lists or strings, in reverse. If you wrap it in a list—like `list(reversed([1, 2, 3]))`—you’ll get a result like `[3, 2, 1]`.
detail: `reversed` itself does not directly modify the original list. This card serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how loop flow and loop tools are executed in actual code. When solving problems, the loop’s starting value, condition, current value of the loop variable, `update` line, and `break` and `continue` conditions are displayed separately.

title: `enumerate` takes both an index and a value
body: `enumerate` is a tool that returns both an index number and the actual value when iterating.
detail: If you write `for i, name in enumerate(names)`, `i` will hold numbers like 0, 1, 2, and `name` will hold the actual values from the list. You can also change the starting index by setting `start=1`. This card serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how looping structures and looping tools work in actual code.

title: A ZIP file bundles multiple lists into a single location.
when_to_show: When reviewing zip, tuple, parallel iteration
body: `zip` groups values at the same positions across multiple lists and iterates over them. Given `names` and `scores`, `zip(names, scores)` pairs names with scores at the corresponding positions.
detail: It is important to note that this does not generate all possible combinations, but rather pairs values at the same positions. This card serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how looping flows and looping tools work in actual code. When solving problems, clearly distinguish the loop’s starting value, the loop condition, the current value of the loop variable, the update line, and the `break` and `continue` conditions.

title: The loop tool starts by reading the current value.
body: When combining iteration tools, the first thing to check is what values are assigned to the variables in the current iteration.
detail: `while` checks whether a condition is `True`; `enumerate` provides both an index and a value; and `zip` pairs values at corresponding positions. `sorted` and `reversed` can be used to change the order of the iteration. This card serves as a supplementary guide to help you understand how loop flow and loop constructs work in actual code.
